title: Bhai Bidhi Chand
hookLine: a former thief turned Sikh, well-known in tradition for recovering the Guru's horses from Lahore in disguise

lines: SKILLS THAT DON'T LOOK GOOD ON A RÉSUMÉ.
cards: Some skills don't look good on a résumé. Moving without a sound. Reading a guard's habits.

Talking your way past a gate. Getting out of a place before anyone notices you're gone. Bhai Bidhi Chand had all of them, and Sikh tradition doesn't pretend otherwise: before he came to the Guru, he was a thief.
The surprise is what happened to those skills afterward. They didn't vanish. They changed owners.

teach.h: A THIEF WHO CAME TO THE GURU.
teach.b: Tradition says Bidhi Chand grew up in a village near Amritsar and fell in with bad company, stealing to live. Then he came into the Guru's circle in the time of Guru Arjan, and his life turned.
He became a Sikh, and later one of Guru Hargobind's trusted companions. Now his well-known story.
Tradition says devoted Sikhs from far to the west were bringing fine horses as an offering to Guru Hargobind, and on the road, officials seized them and sent them to the royal stables in Lahore Fort.
Tradition names the horses Dilbagh and Gulbagh. The Guru's people were upset, and Bidhi Chand said, in effect: leave this to me.

teach.h: A GRASS-CUTTER AND A NIGHTLY SPLASH.
teach.b: He went to Lahore dressed as a grass-cutter, and sold the stables grass so good and so cheap that they hired him to tend the horses. He was patient. He won the grooms' trust.

teach.h: OVER THE WALL, INTO THE RIVER.
teach.b: Every night, the story says, he threw a heavy stone off the fort wall into the river below, until the guards grew used to the splash and stopped looking. Then one night, the splash was him.
He rode the horse over the wall into the water, swam it across, and brought it to the Guru.
For the second horse, tradition says, he came back as a fortune-teller who claimed he could find what had been stolen, and rode off with that one too. Sikhs tell this with a grin.
Under the grin is something serious: the Guru didn't ask Bidhi Chand to become a different man with no past.
He took the cleverness, the nerve, the patience, and turned them toward something true.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Bidhi Chand as one of the companions of Guru Hargobind, remembered for his courage and cleverness after he left a life of theft and came to the Guru.

practice: Ask yourself, honestly: what's a skill I have that I'm a little embarrassed by? Talking people round, finding loopholes, noticing what others miss, getting things done fast and not quite by the book; don't judge it, just name it.
Then picture one way that same skill could help someone, untangling a form, spotting what a friend needs, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
